text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- A commission examining Sweden's housing policy concludes that the state should invest 10 billion crowns in housing over the next 10 years in order to reduce segregation.
- Criticism of Prime Minister Goran Persson's visit to China is growing since the sentence of dissident Wang Dan to 11 years imprisonment. Persson has promised to protest against the sentence.

- Swedish industry is a world leader within four sectors -- pulp and paper, electrical manufacturing, metal goods production and steel production -- surveyed by the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
- The former managing director of Swedish hamburger restaurant chain Clock was convicted of insider trading by a Stockholm court.
- A small development company, Sealcoat, based in the western Swedish city Gothenburg, has tempted former head of Volvo Pehr Gyllenhammar to take a stake in the business.
Hans Rausing, a billionaire from the Tetra Pak packaging group, may also participate, sources say.
- Private health and welfare insurance is seen growing to a multi-billion crown market over the next 10 years as the state dismantles its welfare system.
- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, maintains its positive stance on linking the Swedish crown to Europe's Economic and Monetary Union, but politicians are for the most part against it.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson tells Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin that he sees Russian natural gas as an alternative energy source to Norwegian oil.
- Within a few years telecoms group Ericsson's most important European market will be Germany, where mobile telephones are relatively uncommon.
